---
title: "ReLU"
description: "A piecewise-linear activation function that outputs zero for negative inputs and the input itself for positive values."
term: "ReLU"
letter: "R"
category: "Deep Learning"
difficulty: "Beginner"
---

## Simple explanation

The rectified linear unit (ReLU) keeps positive values and replaces
negative values with zero. It gives neural networks a simple nonlinearity
that helps them learn more than linear transformations alone.

## Technical explanation

ReLU is $f(x)=\max(0,x)$. Its derivative is 1 for positive inputs and 0
for negative inputs; at zero, implementations choose a subgradient
convention. It is computationally inexpensive, but units that remain
negative can stop receiving gradient updates (the “dying ReLU” issue).

## Why it matters in AI engineering

ReLU is a common baseline activation in feed-forward and convolutional
networks. Activation choice influences optimization and output behavior,
and alternatives such as GELU or leaky ReLU may be more appropriate in some
architectures.

## How it works

Applied elementwise to a pre-activation $z$, ReLU returns $z$ when $z>0$
and 0 otherwise. Its zero-valued negative region creates sparse activations,
while its positive region preserves the input magnitude.

## Practical example

A hidden layer can apply ReLU after a learned linear transformation:
$h=\mathrm{ReLU}(Wx+b)$. Stacking such layers allows a network to model
piecewise-linear decision boundaries.

## Common misconceptions

- ReLU is not linear over its entire input range, even though each region
  is linear.
- ReLU is not the only activation and may not be ideal for every layer or
  architecture.
